newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Bush, Carter call for community service.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Bush, Carter call for community service.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, flanked by two former presidents, on Sunday called on Americans to volunteer for community service and then set an example by painting over graffiti in a gritty Philadelphia neighbourhood.

Standing shoulder-to-shoulder with George Bush and Jimmy Carter at the start of a three-day "Presidents' Summit" on volunteerism, Clinton told several thousand people at a battered sports stadium that it was their duty to serve their communities.

"I want to redefine the meaning of citizenship in America," Clinton, dressed in a short-sleeved shirt and khaki work pants, told the volunteers gathered at the Marcus Foster Stadium in north Philadelphia.

"To be a good citizen you have to obey the law, you've got to go to work or be in school, you've got to pay your taxes and -- oh yes -- you've got to serve in your community to help make it a better place," he said.

"This country has produced a lot of jobs in the last four years," he added. "But we're still losing too many kids to crime, to drugs, to not having a decent income ... and we're here because we don't think we have to put up with it."

After the rally, Clinton and Vice President Al Gore, along with their wives Hillary and Tipper, helped paint over graffiti on the outside wall of a building housing an indoor community swimming pool near the stadium.
Recovering from a torn tendon in his right knee, Clinton leaned his crutches against a wall and, standing unaided, used a paint roller on an extended handle to lather the wall with beige paint.
With his wife Hillary, a long-time advocate of programmes for poor children, he sat down with a group of five-year-olds and read to them.

The summit brought a rare show of presidential power, with Clinton, Bush and Carter attending Sunday's rally and former President Gerald Ford and Nancy Reagan, the wife of former President Ronald Reagan, scheduled to join them on Monday.
It placed Clinton side by side with Bush, the man he ousted from the White House in 1992 and whose "Thousand Points of Light" volunteer initiative he ridiculed during that election.

The summit also put Gore next to a man he ardently hopes will not run for the presidency in 2000, Republican Gen. Colin Powell, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff who is chairing the summit.
Bush, Carter and Powell fanned out to different parts of the city to lead clean up patrols, with the retired general picking up trash and liquor bottles in a derelict lot near a crack house.
At the rally, Clinton said the Defence and Transportation Departments would each tutor 1 million children over the next four years, while the government would adopt 2,000 schools.
Despite the demonstration of support from across the political spectrum for the summit, some people bristled at the idea of the government encouraging people to volunteer.
Several dozen student protesters greeted Clinton at the stadium with signs saying "Don't Volunteer Me."

And Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell, who strongly supports the summit but has criticised federal welfare cuts, said the spotlight on volunteerism should not obscure a continued need for the government to address major social issues.

"Volunteerism is very helpful when it's designed for things like mentoring youth, safe places to play after school, but volunteerism can't solve everything," he told reporters before the rally. "Government still has a significant role, if not the most significant role to play," he added.

On Sunday evening, Clinton was to attend a musical gala and to give Presidential Service Awards to 10 people. On Monday, he will speak at the summit's main session, along with the former presidents, before returning to Washington.
